name: The Motion Aftereffect
statement: Stare at a waterfall, then at the rocks beside it, and the still rocks seem to drift upward.
statementAccent: the still rocks seem to drift upward
meaning: The motion aftereffect is a visual illusion experienced after viewing a moving stimulus steadily for a while, typically thirty to sixty seconds, and then looking at a stationary scene: the stationary scene appears to move in the direction opposite to the previously viewed motion. Its most famous demonstration gives it the name the waterfall illusion, from the observation that staring at a waterfall and then looking at the adjacent stationary rocks makes them appear to drift upward. The effect was described in 1834 by Robert Addams after he observed the Falls of Foyers in Scotland, with an ancient antecedent in Aristotle's report of illusory motion after watching a flowing river. The motion aftereffect is a classic and important illusion in vision science, taken as direct evidence that the brain contains neurons selective for the direction of motion, and it has been localised to the motion-processing area of the visual cortex known as MT or V5.
mechanism: The effect arises from neural adaptation of direction-selective motion detectors. The visual cortex contains populations of neurons each tuned to motion in a particular direction, and perceived motion reflects the balance of activity across these populations. When you view motion in one direction for a prolonged period, the neurons tuned to that direction adapt, reducing their response, while neurons tuned to the opposite direction are relatively unaffected. When you then look at a stationary scene, all these neurons return toward their baseline firing, but because the neurons for the adapted direction are temporarily depressed, the population signal is now unbalanced in favour of the opposite direction, and the brain interprets this imbalance as motion the opposite way. Modern neuroscience confirms the account: functional imaging shows the illusion engages the motion area MT, or V5, and stimulating that area can disrupt the aftereffect. A curious signature of the illusion is that the scene appears to move yet does not change position, a paradoxical percept of motion without displacement.

examples.text: Staring at falling water and then at the neighbouring stationary rocks makes the rocks appear to drift upward, opposite to the water's downward flow.
During the aftereffect the scene seems to move yet its features do not change position, a paradoxical percept of movement without going anywhere.
Functional imaging shows the aftereffect engages the motion-processing area MT, or V5, evidence for direction-selective neurons in the brain.

variants.name: Direction-selective adaptation
variants.text: The mechanism by which prolonged motion in one direction fatigues neurons tuned to it, unbalancing the population signal toward the opposite direction.

variants.name: Motion without displacement
variants.text: The paradoxical percept in which the adapted scene appears to move while its features remain in place, going nowhere.

whyItMatters: The motion aftereffect is a classic and important illusion in vision science, historically providing some of the first psychophysical evidence that the brain analyses motion with neurons specifically tuned to direction. By showing that adapting to motion in one direction produces illusory motion in the opposite direction, it revealed the existence of direction-selective motion channels and demonstrated feature-specific neural adaptation, a landmark in understanding how the visual system is organised. Modern neuroscience has confirmed and localised the effect, tying it to the motion area MT, or V5, and using it to probe how motion is represented and adapted in the cortex. The illusion also poses a deep puzzle in the paradox of motion without displacement, which continues to inform theories of how motion and position are computed. Simple to demonstrate yet rich in implications, it remains a cornerstone example of adaptation and motion perception.

working.text: view motion in a single direction steadily for perhaps a minute, so the neurons tuned to that direction adapt and respond less.
shift to a stationary scene, where the depressed neurons leave the population signal unbalanced toward the opposite direction.
experience the still scene appearing to move the opposite way, a motion aftereffect localised to area MT.

limits: The motion aftereffect requires prolonged adaptation to consistent motion and is temporary, fading over seconds to minutes as the adapted neurons recover. Its strength depends on the duration, speed, and contrast of the adapting motion and on the properties of the test stimulus, and it varies across observers. The effect is direction-specific and reflects adaptation in motion-processing neurons rather than a general failure of vision. Some historical attributions, such as an ancient description by Lucretius, are uncertain, though Addams's 1834 account and Aristotle's antecedent are firm. The paradoxical percept of motion without position change is genuine but still not fully explained. So the illusion reliably demonstrates direction-selective adaptation and the neural basis of motion perception, within the specific conditions of prolonged adaptation, while some of its features remain subjects of research.
misreadings: The illusory motion is not real movement of the scene; the stationary features do not actually move or change position, which is exactly the paradox. The effect is not eye fatigue in general but adaptation of specific direction-selective neurons, so it is direction-specific and reverses the adapting motion. And it is temporary, fading as the neurons recover, so treating the aftereffect as the scene truly moving, or as generic tiredness of the eyes, misreads a phenomenon that reveals the brain's dedicated motion-detecting machinery.
origin: Described in 1834 by Robert Addams after observing the Falls of Foyers in Scotland, with an ancient antecedent in Aristotle; now understood as adaptation of direction-selective neurons in the motion area MT or V5.
